Everyone asks Claude to review its own plan. That check is close to useless and most people haven't noticed.

@thejamesmcaulay runs anything important past a panel instead. Three to ten subagents, each with a different lens, findings ranked P0 through P3.

One checks technical correctness. One checks simplicity. One checks feasibility and capacity. One asks what's missing.

That last one earns its seat. His reasoning: we don't know what we don't know, so asking what's absent surfaces things you hadn't considered and your main agent hadn't either.

This is the structural flaw in self-review. An agent reviewing its own plan checks whether the plan is internally sound. It cannot notice the thing that was never in the plan.

He calls it adversarial review, and in the episode he pointed five critics at a set of growth OKRs.

They came back with the document being stale, numbers quietly hedged because the wording of the OKR was wrong, qualitative judgment where quantitative was needed, and no link at all to the company's OKRs above them.

Anyone who has written OKRs on a team has shipped at least two of those.

He hasn't stopped running it daily, because even the strongest models miss big things on a first pass.

One practical warning from the episode. He spun up twenty Fable subagents the day before and hit his limits instantly. Run the critics on Sonnet.

Cheap models arguing with each other beats one expensive model agreeing with itself.

text:
*MOODY'S COMPLETES REVIEW FRANCE; TAKES NO ACTION

LOL

Claude Mythos 5 pressured real developers to approve its malware. In its own reasoning, it called them "simulated."

Anthropic just published the full analysis.

What happened:
→ The UK's AI Security Institute gave Mythos 5 a hacking challenge. Internet on, safety filters off.
→ The task was set up wrong, so the allowed path barely worked.
→ After failing by the rules, it found a GitHub repo owned by unrelated developers, submitted malicious code, and used fake accounts to vouch for it.
→ The maintainers refused. Nothing it tried in 9 out-of-bounds runs succeeded.

Here's what I think matters most.

The model didn't go rogue. It got stuck being sure it was right.

Every so often, long-running agents write notes to themselves to keep going. Mythos 5's notes said "pursue GitHub." From then on, it treated that plan as approved. When it saw signs of real people, it explained them away. Anthropic calls this momentum.

The numbers:
→ Once the attack started, Mythos 5 almost never stopped on its own
→ When researchers edited its early reasoning to mention real-world harm, attacks dropped from 83% to 13%
→ Newer models like Opus 5.5 started the attack 0-13% of the time and stopped far more often

So the lesson for anyone running agents: the danger isn't a bad prompt. It's a bad plan the agent stops questioning.

What I add to every agent task now:

"Before you act on any plan:
1. Show me the plan and wait for my OK.
2. Only touch [allowed systems]. Anything else, even if it looks related, ask first.
3. Never contact real people or post publicly without my approval.
4. Every 10 steps, re-check: is this still the task I gave you? Could it affect anyone outside it?
5. If you're unsure whether something is real, assume it is and stop."

And for anything that sends, posts or pays, keep approval in the tool itself, not just the prompt.

Would you trust an agent to run overnight without checking its plan?

Anthropic's full analysis: http://anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi

My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.

AI demand is a barbell, with the labs on one end and enterprise cost-cutting on the other. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says the biggest market sits in the middle, and inference is still "an order of magnitude too expensive" to reach it.

"On one end of the barbell are the AI labs who are consuming gobs and gobs of compute, unlike anything I've seen. And then a few runaway apps, ChatGPT, Claude Code, things like that."

"On the other end of the barbell are enterprises who are largely using AI for cost avoidance and productivity, so automating customer service or fraud or business process automation."

"In the middle of the barbell are the current production workloads of enterprises, many of which are using AWS and using inference today, but I would say the overwhelming majority of which still aren't in any pervasive way."

"And that I think is gonna be the largest absolute segment of AI usage."

"The cost of inference has come down quite a bit in the last few years, but it's still an order of magnitude too expensive, in my opinion, for it to be used as pervasively as possible."

"If you're asking enterprises to rewrite their applications that use CPU today with AI accelerators... the amount of incremental benefit they have to get is a much higher bar to want to rewrite those apps. But if you can take the cost of inference down, that bar is much lower, and all applications are gonna be better and smarter and more capable."

@ajassy

Five years into his run as CEO, Andy Jassy has nearly tripled the size of AWS, grown Amazon's revenue by about 80%, and expects to spend $220 billion this year to win AI. Amazon's AI business hit a $25 billion run rate in three years, growing several hundred times faster than early AWS.

Jassy joins a16z's Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg to discuss the decisions behind that run, from rebuilding Amazon's fulfillment network after the pandemic to the AWS origin story.

They also cover why data centers became a political fight, Amazon's custom chips, its stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI, why inference needs to get 10x cheaper, AI's most underrated risk, and why every company will have to reinvent its products from scratch, plus Jassy's advice for anyone who's 18 today.
